lesson.title: Counting Derivatives with Tick Marks
lesson.summary: Explains Lagrange's prime notation for first and higher derivatives, then computes a second derivative from the limit definition to show what those extra tick marks actually measure.
lesson.body:
Prime notation, introduced by the mathematician Joseph Louis Lagrange, marks a derivative with a small tick after the function's name: f prime of x for the first derivative, and it extends naturally to repeated differentiation, since the derivative of a function is itself a function and can be differentiated again. Differentiating f prime of x produces the second derivative, written f double prime of x, and differentiating that produces the third derivative, f triple prime of x. Beyond three tick marks the notation usually switches to a number in parentheses, such as f superscript (4) of x for the fourth derivative, since a row of tick marks becomes hard to read.

The appeal of prime notation is its compactness: it lets you refer to "the function," "its derivative," and "the derivative of that" without introducing new letters or writing out dy divided by dx repeatedly. It also reads naturally when a function is used to model something concrete, since f prime of a and f double prime of a can both be evaluated as specific numbers at a chosen point, just like f of a itself.

Work through an example using f(x) = x cubed, whose first derivative was already found by the limit definition to be f prime of x = 3 x squared. To find the second derivative, apply the same limit definition to g(x) = 3 x squared: f double prime of x equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [3(x + h) squared minus 3 x squared] divided by h. Expanding (x + h) squared gives x squared plus 2xh plus h squared, so 3 times that is 3 x squared plus 6xh plus 3h squared. Subtracting 3 x squared leaves 6xh plus 3h squared, and dividing by h gives 6x plus 3h. Letting h approach 0 leaves f double prime of x equals 6x.

Now evaluate both derivatives at x = 2: f prime of 2 equals 3 times 4, which is 12, matching the earlier point computation exactly, and f double prime of 2 equals 6 times 2, which is 12 as well, a coincidence of this particular function and point rather than a general rule. The second derivative measures how the first derivative itself is changing, in this case how fast the slope of the tangent line is increasing as x grows, which later becomes the basis for describing concavity.

Higher derivatives are not just a notational exercise. In the position and velocity language from earlier, if s(t) gives position, then s prime of t gives velocity, and s double prime of t gives acceleration, the rate at which velocity itself is changing. Applying the same limit definition used above to any position function produces its acceleration function automatically, which is part of why physics leans so heavily on derivatives: one differentiation turns position into velocity, and a second turns velocity into acceleration, both computed by the identical limit, just applied one more time.

Prime notation has one limitation worth flagging: it does not show which variable the differentiation is being taken with respect to, since f prime of x only makes sense once you already know x is the input variable. When a formula involves several letters, that ambiguity becomes a real problem, and it is exactly the gap that Leibniz notation, covered next, was built to close.
